fao_fpi.label: FAO Food Price Index and five groups (monthly)

peak_estimate.note: The current level is already above every analogue on these same days, so both adding and multiplying their gain lead beyond anything measured (record of the series +3.02 °C). The real question is not how much higher but when the growth stops: for the analogues that happened in November or December.

breakdown.note: per issue: models whose nearest verifiable forecast came in below the ONI that season actually had

todate.note: the models forecast a three-month mean; this compares them with the part of that season already measured, so a model below this number would need the rest of the season to be colder than the part already lived

risks.title: A very strong El Niño is under way
risks.evidence: Niño 3.4 by the NOAA weekly index +2.6 °C on 2026-08-26; daily OISST +2.58. Among all years since 1982 for the same 30 days: rank 1.
risks.plain: Water in the key patch of the Pacific is 2.6 degrees warmer than normal. The threshold for a “very strong” event is two degrees. This is not a forecast, it is already measured, and it has never happened this early in the year.
risks.watch: the NOAA weekly index; the official ONI is now +1.39 (MJJ), the “very strong” category starts at +2.0 on the three-month average

risks.title: The strongest part is still ahead
risks.evidence: Past analogues peaked in November to January. Adding their gain from the same date gives +3.4 … +4.5 °C, above the record of the series +3.02.
risks.plain: Every past event of this strength peaked in winter, November to January. It is the end of summer now, so two or three more months of growth are likely. How much higher cannot be said: we are already above anything the ocean has shown at this time of year, and past events are no guide here. The real question is when the growth stops.
risks.watch: if the weekly Niño 3.4 stops rising before November, the event has reached its plateau earlier than the analogues

risks.title: The eastern Pacific is heating, off the coast of South America
risks.plain: There are two kinds of El Niño: one heats the middle of the ocean, the other the east, off Peru and Ecuador. This is the second kind, the harshest in its consequences: 1982 and 1997 were like this. Such events brought downpours and floods to the coast of South America and droughts to Indonesia and Australia.
risks.watch: the difference staying above 1 °C through September and October

risks.title: The world ocean is warmer every day than it has ever been on that day
risks.evidence: 30 record days out of the last 30, a run of 30 days in a row; 90 of 229 days this year.
risks.plain: On each of the last 30 days the ocean, averaged over the planet, was warmer than on the same day of any year since 1982. Not one hot day, but an unbroken stretch.
risks.watch: the first day below the record without a change of season is the first sign of a turn

risks.title: Niño 3.4: not a spike but a new level
risks.evidence: accumulated shift +149 against a threshold of 5; first over the threshold 107 days ago
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 107 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go

risks.title: The year after the peak: 2027 is likely to be warmer than 2026
risks.evidence: In 1982→1983 +0.19 °C, 1997→1998 +0.19 °C, 2015→2016 +0.18 °C, 2023→2024 +0.12 °C (annual land+ocean mean, ERA5); warmer in 4 of 4 analogues, median +0.19.
risks.plain: El Niño releases the ocean's heat into the air with a lag of a few months, so the calendar year that follows the peak is usually the warmer one. That is why 1998, 2016 and 2024 each became the warmest year measured up to that point. On the same arithmetic, next year is the one to plan for, not this one.
risks.watch: annual land+ocean mean once the peak passes; the first months of next year already carry the signal

risks.title: world ocean: not a spike but a new level
risks.evidence: accumulated shift +55 against a threshold of 5; first over the threshold 55 days ago
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 55 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go

risks.title: land+ocean: not a spike but a new level
risks.evidence: accumulated shift +30 against a threshold of 5; first over the threshold 32 days ago
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 32 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go

risks.title: world ocean: the last 30 days are the warmest in the whole record
risks.plain: For these same dates none of the 45 years was warmer. Even after subtracting the general warming, +0.32 degrees remain above it: that is what the event itself adds.
risks.watch: whether the lead holds after the change of season

risks.title: land+ocean: the last 30 days are the warmest in the whole record
risks.plain: For these same dates none of the 87 years was warmer. Even after subtracting the general warming, +0.52 degrees remain above it: that is what the event itself adds.
risks.watch: whether the lead holds after the change of season

risks.title: Some forecast models are already below reality
risks.evidence: 10 of 26 models gave less for ASO than the already reached +2.6 °C: CPC MRKOV, CS-IRI-MM, CSU CLIPR, IAP-NN, IOCAS ICM, JAMSTEC CNN…. Model mean +2.77, spread +1.60…+3.75.
risks.plain: Of 26 models, 10 have already fallen behind what the ocean showed this week. They are not “wrong about the future”; they are not keeping up with the present. Their winter forecasts are most likely too low.
risks.watch: the next IRI issue: how many models catch up

metric.name: Combined forecast peak by IRI issue

risks.title: The models are revising the forecast upward for the second month running
risks.evidence: Since the Jul 2026 issue 25 of 25 models raised their peak, 0 lowered it; combined peak +2.95 → +3.25 °C.
risks.plain: When almost all models move their forecast in the same direction, the event is outrunning them. The shift itself is a signal: the next issue will probably be higher again.

metric.name: Combined forecast peak by IRI issue

risks.title: A La Niña usually follows within a year or two
risks.evidence: After the analogues the ONI fell to 1982: -1.06, 1997: -1.53, 2015: -0.76, 2023: -0.61; it crossed the La Niña threshold of −0.5 in 4 of 4 cases.
risks.plain: The ocean does not simply return to normal: after a strong El Niño it usually swings the other way. A La Niña flips the map of impacts, so the regions that are dry now tend to be wet then, and the grain exporters that had a good year tend to have a bad one. Planning that only covers this winter misses the swing.
risks.watch: the ONI trend after the peak; a fall of 0.3 or more per month is the usual signature of the swing

risks.title: The impacts of this peak land mostly next year
risks.evidence: Land+ocean is +0.52 °C above trend now, while the ocean heat that drives it is still rising; in the analogues the air-temperature records, the harvest failures and the price effects all came in the year after the onset.
risks.plain: The dashboard measures the ocean today, but people meet an El Niño through harvests, water and prices, and those arrive with a delay of six to eighteen months. The plans that matter are for next year: import contracts, reserves, water rationing, insurance.
risks.watch: the first harvests after the peak season and the food price index six to twelve months from the onset

risks.title: Data “Niño 3.4, the El Niño focus (OISST)” is lagging
risks.plain: The daily series is 18 days behind: the source publishes with a delay. While it is silent, the watchdog sees the past on this series; the NOAA weekly data is fresher and shows everything.

risks.title: Data “Ocean, 60°S–60°N (OISST)” is lagging
risks.plain: The daily series is 18 days behind: the source publishes with a delay. While it is silent, the watchdog sees the past on this series; the NOAA weekly data is fresher and shows everything.

food.note: FAO Food Price Index, 2014–16 = 100; published the first Friday of the month for the previous month.

season_notes.SON: September-October-November. The season when El Niño is building towards its peak: the teleconnections are already switched on, and in the southern hemisphere it is the planting season.
season_notes.DJF: December-January-February. The peak season of almost every El Niño and the strongest teleconnections: the southern African and Australian summer, the northern winter.
season_notes.MAM: March-April-May. The decaying phase: the ocean is still warm, and the food consequences of the peak season arrive as harvests and prices.

base.what: the event peaks near the middle of the plume

strong.what: the event peaks at the top of the model spread

record.what: the peak goes above the record of the weekly NOAA series

scenario_support._note: Share of the 26 IRI models whose peak reaches the threshold. Not a probability: these are 26 different models, not draws from one. Reality is already above 4 of them, so every share here is a lower bound.

items.name: Gulf and Arabian Peninsula
items.countries: UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Yemen

SON.note: The winter rain season has not started; no consistent signal.

DJF.note: El Niño strengthens the subtropical jet over Arabia, and winter rainfall runs above normal: the documented pathway behind heavy-rain and flash-flood episodes on the peninsula, including the April 2024 Gulf floods.

MAM.note: The wet tendency fades through spring; heat arrives early.

vulnerability.note: The Gulf states import 80–90 % of their food and grow almost no cereals: the exposure is entirely to world prices, shipping and the harvests of exporters. Yemen combines that dependence with an ongoing food emergency.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

items.name: East Africa
items.countries: Kenya, Somalia, southern Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda

SON.note: Short rains (Oct–Dec) usually well above normal; flooding and landslides, and conditions that favour desert locust breeding.

DJF.note: The wet tail of the short rains runs into January; standing water and disease follow.

MAM.note: The long rains show no consistent El Niño signal.

vulnerability.note: Large food-insecure population; cereal imports are 20–40 % of consumption in Kenya and Somalia; floods hit pastoral and lowland cropping areas hardest.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

items.name: Southern Africa
items.countries: Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Botswana, Namibia

SON.note: A late and weak start of the rainy season delays planting.

DJF.note: The main maize season runs drier and hotter than normal: 1982-83, 1991-92, 2015-16 and 2023-24 all brought regional maize failures.

MAM.note: Rains end early and the harvest is cut short.

vulnerability.note: Maize-dependent diets and thin reserves; Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia declared drought emergencies in 2024.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.
Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

items.name: Pacific Islands
items.countries: Fiji, Papua New Guinea highlands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Micronesia

SON.note: The western Pacific (PNG, Fiji, Vanuatu) runs dry while the central Pacific (Kiribati, Tuvalu) is much wetter; sea level drops in the west and exposes reefs.

DJF.note: Drought in the west persists, and tropical cyclone activity shifts east towards French Polynesia and the Cooks.

vulnerability.note: Small islands import most staples and depend on shipping; the 1997-98 event brought famine conditions to the PNG highlands.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

items.countries: Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Haiti, Cuba, Dominican Republic

SON.note: The dry corridor (Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua) runs dry and the second bean and maize crop is at risk.

DJF.note: The Caribbean is drier than normal.

MAM.note: A late start of the first rainy season.

vulnerability.note: Haiti and the dry-corridor countries combine high import dependence with chronic food insecurity and out-migration.

items.name: Southeast Asia and Indonesia
items.countries: Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea

SON.note: A delayed monsoon onset, drought and peat fires in Indonesia and Malaysia; the Philippines run dry.

DJF.note: Reduced rainfall persists; rice and palm-oil yields fall and Philippine drought deepens.

MAM.note: A dry tail: reservoirs low, hydropower reduced.

vulnerability.note: Rice self-sufficiency is thin in Indonesia and the Philippines, and both import in El Niño years; Thailand and Vietnam are exporters whose smaller crops raise world prices.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

items.name: Peru, Ecuador and the Andes

SON.note: Coastal Ecuador and northern Peru begin to see heavy rain; the coastal El Niño effect is strongest in eastern-type events.

DJF.note: Torrential rain and floods on the Peruvian and Ecuadorian coast, as in 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2017; the anchoveta fishery collapses while the Bolivian altiplano and the southern Peruvian Andes run dry.

MAM.note: Coastal floods persist through the southern autumn, with landslides and disease outbreaks.

vulnerability.note: Peru imports wheat and maize; fishmeal exports and coastal agriculture (rice, mango, asparagus) are hit directly, and Colombia and Bolivia rely on imported wheat.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
Prepare for a collapse of coastal upwelling fisheries: fishing bans, income support, alternative supply of fish protein.

items.countries: Mali, Niger, Chad, Burkina Faso, Senegal, Sudan

SON.note: The rainy season (Jul–Sep) tends to be weaker in El Niño years; by September it is mostly over, so the effect is already in the standing crop.

vulnerability.note: The highest structural food insecurity, conflict, and cereal imports of 30–60 % of consumption in Mauritania and Senegal; any price shock becomes a crisis.

items.countries: Egypt, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Iran

SON.note: No consistent signal at the start of the wet season.

DJF.note: The eastern Mediterranean and Iraq–Iran tend to be wetter; north-west Africa shows a mixed and weaker response.

MAM.note: No consistent signal; local drought there is driven more by the Atlantic than by the Pacific.

vulnerability.note: The world's largest wheat importers: Egypt, Algeria and Morocco import 50–75 % of their cereals, and Lebanon and Jordan more. Exposure runs through world prices and the harvests of the Black Sea exporters.

items.name: South Asia
items.countries: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal

SON.note: The monsoon withdraws earlier; the north-east monsoon is mixed, and southern India and Sri Lanka are often wetter.

DJF.note: A warmer and drier winter in northern India and Pakistan; the rabi wheat crop is exposed to March heat.

MAM.note: Pre-monsoon heat waves become more likely.

vulnerability.note: Largely self-sufficient in cereals but with a huge population close to the margin; India restricts exports in bad years, and that alone moves world rice prices.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

items.name: East Asia

SON.note: Southern China is somewhat wetter in autumn.

DJF.note: A wetter winter in southern China and a milder winter in Japan and Korea.

MAM.note: A wetter spring in south China; the following summer often brings Yangtze flooding, as in 1998 and 2016.

vulnerability.note: China holds large reserves but is the largest soybean and a major maize importer; Japan and Korea import most of their cereals but are wealthy enough to secure them.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

items.name: Southern Cone
items.countries: southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, northern Argentina; north-east Brazil

SON.note: Southern Brazil, Uruguay and north-east Argentina run wetter, with floods in the Paraná basin, while north-east Brazil runs dry.

DJF.note: A wet summer favourable for Argentine soybean and maize once the floods drain; north-east Brazil stays in drought.

MAM.note: A wet autumn delays the harvest.

vulnerability.note: Net exporters of soybean, maize and wheat: the world-price effect is usually favourable because the crops are bigger, and the local risk is floods and the north-eastern drought.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

items.name: Australia and New Zealand
items.countries: eastern and northern Australia, New Zealand

SON.note: Spring is drier and hotter in the east and north; the winter crop finishes badly and the bushfire season starts early.

DJF.note: A hot, dry summer in the east, bushfires, and a delayed northern wet season.

vulnerability.note: A major wheat exporter: a poor Australian crop tightens the world wheat balance and raises prices for importers elsewhere.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

items.name: North America

SON.note: Weak autumn signals; the Atlantic hurricane season is usually suppressed.

DJF.note: The southern tier from California to Florida runs wetter, the northern US and Canada warmer and drier; the Pacific North-west and the Ohio valley run dry.

MAM.note: A wet spring in the southern Plains and the Gulf, which is good for winter wheat.

vulnerability.note: The largest maize and soybean exporter; El Niño winters are usually favourable for US crops, which eases world supply.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

items.name: West Africa (Gulf of Guinea)

SON.note: No consistent signal for the second rainy season.

MAM.note: A weak and mixed signal at the start of the first rainy season.

vulnerability.note: Rice and wheat imports matter (Nigeria, Ghana); the exposure runs through world prices rather than local weather.

actions: No strong signal: watch the neighbours' harvests and world prices rather than local weather.

items.name: Europe

SON.note: Autumn shows no reliable El Niño signal over Europe.

DJF.note: Early winter is dominated by the North Atlantic, not the Pacific: the El Niño signal is weak and inconsistent between events.

MAM.note: Late winter and early spring carry the clearest, still weak, signal: a stratospheric pathway that tends towards a negative North Atlantic Oscillation, which usually means colder and drier northern Europe and wetter southern Europe and the Mediterranean.

vulnerability.note: A net exporter of cereals overall and wealthy enough to outbid others on the world market; the risk here is price, not availability. A poor southern-European harvest raises world prices for the importers elsewhere.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

items.name: Russia and Central Asia
items.countries: European Russia, Siberia, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan

SON.note: No reliable signal for the autumn sowing of winter wheat.

DJF.note: Winters in European Russia tend to be milder in El Niño years, but the effect is small next to the Atlantic and Arctic drivers and does not repeat reliably.

MAM.note: Central Asia (Kazakhstan to Tajikistan) tends towards a wetter winter and spring, which is favourable for the grain crop; for Russia itself the spring signal is not distinguishable from noise.

vulnerability.note: Russia and Kazakhstan are among the largest wheat exporters: what matters for the world is their harvest, not their imports. A poor Black Sea crop is the single fastest route from weather to global bread prices.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
sources: ENSO signal over Russia and Central Asia is weak and season-dependent: Brönnimann 2007; NOAA CPC composite maps; Central Asian winter-spring precipitation response documented in regional studies (Barlow et al.)

regions.method: level = round(0.6 × impact + 0.4 × vulnerability + scenario), clipped to 1–5; impact: robust 4, likely 3, weak 1.5, none 0; scenario: base +0 (the event as in the combined forecast), strong +0.5 (top of the model spread), record +1 (reality above every model); one point lower everywhere if the combined peak is below 1.5 °C.

summary.verdict: ALERT: Niño 3 is above anything measured at +3.4 °C, against the previous maximum of +3.3 °C. Niño 3.4 is at +2.6 °C weekly and above all analogues for this date.

turning_point.why: No. The 30-day mean of Niño 3.4 rose from +2.43 °C to +2.44 °C, while the world ocean 30-day mean stayed at +0.73 °C. The last daily Niño 3.4 eased only +0.02 °C, from +2.60 to +2.58, not a turn.

summary.changed: Niño 3.4 advanced one day to 2026-08-16; last day +2.58 °C (was +2.60), 30-day anomaly +2.44 (was +2.43). World ocean advanced one day; last day +0.73 °C (was +0.74), 30-day anomaly +0.73 (was +0.73). Land+ocean had no new days and still ends on 2026-08-26.
summary.outlook_2_3w: Niño 3.4: from +2.58 °C the 14-day forecast middle (p50) is +2.52 °C, low (p10) +2.25 °C, high (p90) +2.90 °C; analogue middle +2.52 °C. World ocean: middle +0.732 °C, high +0.798 °C. Land+ocean: middle +1.016 °C, high +1.151 °C. No forecast path shows cooling over the next two to three weeks; the event should remain at record-level warmth.
watch: Daily Niño 3.4 moving toward the low forecast path +2.25 °C (p10) instead of the middle +2.52 °C (p50).
The 30-day record run of Niño 3.4 breaking: it currently has 30 records in the last 30 days.
NOAA weekly eastern Pacific flattening: the four-week change of +0.4 °C in Niño 1+2 or +0.6 °C in Niño 3 turning negative.
World ocean daily value moving toward its low forecast path +0.685 °C (p10).
Next IRI issue: fewer than 25 of 25 models raising their peak, or the combined peak stopping at +3.28 °C.
summary.confidence: High for the next 2–3 weeks: the coolest forecast path for Niño 3.4 (p10) is +2.25 °C, still above the +2.0 °C very-strong threshold.
caveats: The daily Niño 3.4 and world ocean series are 18 days behind; land+ocean is 8 days behind.
Current Niño 3.4 30-day level +2.44 °C is above the strongest analogues on the same days (2015 +1.47 °C, 1997 +1.57 °C), so analogues cannot bound the peak.
The IRI peak has been revised upward from +2.45 in June to +2.95 in July to +3.28 in August, so model numbers may still be too low.

blocks.C: Niño 3.4 has a 30-day mean of +2.44 °C; the same 30 days in the strongest analogues were +0.73 (1982), +1.57 (1997), +1.47 (2015), +1.16 (2023), so this event ranks 1 among 45 years. The official three-month ONI for May–July (MJJ) is +1.39, above the analogues at the same season (+0.73 to +1.19). NOAA classifies the current weekly pattern as eastern Pacific, canonical.
blocks.D: The risk index is 95 out of 100. Level 5 risk: a very strong El Niño is already measured, with weekly Niño 3.4 at +2.6 °C versus the very-strong threshold of +2.0 °C. Level 4 risks add that the strongest part is still ahead (8–16 weeks), the eastern Pacific is heating, and the world ocean has been warmer than any same day for 30 consecutive days.
blocks.E: The August IRI issue has 26 models. For the current ASO season the combined forecast is +2.75 °C, while the weekly reality is already +2.6 °C, and 10 of 26 models are below reality. The combined peak has been revised upward from +2.45 in June to +2.95 in July to +3.28 in August; 25 of 25 models raised their peak, none lowered it. Since 10 models are already behind the present and the peak was revised upward in consecutive issues, the winter numbers should be read as a lower bound.
blocks.G: Niño 3.4 has a 7-day mean of +2.577 °C and has set a record on each of the last 30 days. The 14-day forecast from +2.58 °C has a middle estimate (p50) of +2.524 °C, low (p10) of +2.248 °C, high (p90) of +2.904 °C; the analogue middle is +2.518 °C. World ocean (60°S–60°N) and global land+ocean also show 30-day record runs, with 30-day means of +0.735 °C and +0.818 °C, and 14-day forecast middle estimates of +0.732 °C and +1.016 °C.
